questions.question: What must a topic sentence do for its paragraph?
questions.solution: State the paragraph's single controlling idea — everything after must support it; anything unrelated belongs elsewhere. It usually opens the paragraph but can sit mid-paragraph or at the end; the test is whether it governs the rest. One paragraph, one idea.

questions.question: A paragraph uses 'however, therefore, moreover' correctly but still reads disconnected. What is missing?
questions.solution: Coherence — the LOGICAL ORDER of ideas. Connectives provide cohesion (surface links), but if the ideas themselves are out of sequence (general → specific, cause → effect, chronological), no linker can save it. Fix the order first, then link.

questions.question: How does narrative writing differ from descriptive writing in purpose and technique?
questions.solution: Narrative TELLS WHAT HAPPENED: events in time order, plot, characters, tension, a sequence of actions (past tense dominates). Descriptive CREATES A PICTURE: sensory details (sight, sound, smell), spatial order, imagery and adjectives, no required events. Narrative moves through time; descriptive freezes a moment and zooms in.

questions.question: Correct the punctuation: she said i am tired and left
questions.solution: 'She said, "I am tired," and left.' Rules: comma before the quoted speech, quotation marks around the exact words, capital letter starting the quote, and the closing punctuation inside the quotes when it belongs to the speech. Dialogue tags frame the quotation — they are not part of it.

questions.question: Name three ways to develop a paragraph after its topic sentence.
questions.solution: (1) EXAMPLES — concrete instances proving the point. (2) CAUSE AND EFFECT — why something happens and what follows. (3) COMPARISON/CONTRAST — lining the idea up against another to clarify it. (Also: definition, process/steps, anecdote.) A paragraph is developed by ELABORATING the topic sentence with one of these patterns, not by adding loosely related sentences.

questions.concept: Why a letter's format carries meaning
questions.question: Why does a job application letter need a formal salutation and structure while a message to a friend does not?
questions.solution: Format encodes the relationship and the purpose: a formal layout signals that the reader is assessing you and that the text is a record, so it must be impersonal, complete and correctly ordered. An informal message signals closeness, where brevity is friendly. Using the wrong format sends a social signal that contradicts your intent — the reader notices the mismatch before the content.

questions.question: A paragraph can use 'however', 'therefore' and 'moreover' in every sentence and still be incoherent. Why?
questions.solution: Cohesion is surface linking — connectives, pronouns, repetition. Coherence is logical organisation: the sentences must actually follow from one another and serve one controlling idea. Connectives can only LABEL relationships; they cannot create one that is absent, so an illogical sequence with good linking words is still incoherent. Fix the reasoning first, then the signposts.

questions.concept: Why editing must be separated from drafting
questions.question: Why does trying to write perfect sentences on the first pass produce worse writing than drafting and then editing?
questions.solution: Drafting and editing use conflicting attention: drafting needs flow of ideas, editing needs critical distance on structure and clarity. Attempting both simultaneously stalls the flow and fixes local phrasing before the argument is settled, so later restructuring wastes the polish. Separating passes lets each be done well — write to discover, edit to decide.
